Improving gaze-tracking technology by enhancing its speed and eﬀectiveness makes it more adaptable as well as user-friendly [11,15,17].

## 3 Methods

The study used a counterbalanced within-subjects repeated measures design to compare the usability of hypothetical ASL input via a Wizard-of-Oz design with that of LLM-assisted touch interfaces, and a variation of LLM-assisted touch via hands-free headpointing. We recruited 23 participants who were all 18 years of age or older, primarily communicated in ASL, and self-identiﬁed as DHH.

### 3.1 Materials

The participants interacted with an Amazon Echo Show device across the three conditions using the three diﬀerent input methods, completing usability questionnaires after each condition. The key quantitative metrics used were psychometrically validated ASL versions of the System Usability Scale (SUS) and Net Promoter Score (NPS) [2], alongside post-experiment survey questions about participant preferences. The SUS measures overall usability along ten dimensions, while NPS provides information about how enthusiastic participants are about a system, and how likely they are to recommend it to others. As mentioned earlier, we utilized a Wizard-of-Oz setup for the ASL condition.

For implementing the LLM Touch and headpointing options, we used an earlier version of the of the code by DeVries et al. [5]. A web-based interface running on a tablet uses past context to ask ChatGPT for appropriate action verbs, which are then interactively reﬁned through the user selecting options in a 3x3 grid of buttons, for a maximum of four steps. The ﬁnal command is issued to the IPA via text-to-speech. Headpointing is a built-in motor accessibility feature on MacOS, which can be used in place of clicking a mouse or touching the screen to select actions. For this option, we presented the LLM Touch interface to our

## 4 Results

### 4.1 Quantitative Results

The results for SUS and NPS are shown in Fig. 2. SUS results for ASL showed excellent usability with a mean SUS score of 79.8 (SD 16.0, SE 3.330). The touch modality received a similar score of 73.2 (SD 16.6, SE 3.451). Head-pointing recorded a much lower average with a SUS of 55.4 (SD 21.2, SE 4.431). The between-groups ANOVA on the SUS scores was statistically signiﬁcant with F(2, 66) = 11.1496 and p < 0.001. Post-hoc paired t-testing with Bonferroni’s correction demonstrated statistically signiﬁcant diﬀerences between ASL and Head-Pointing and between Touch and Head-Pointing, but not between ASL and Touch.

The NPS shows large diﬀerences across the three conditions. This deﬁes predictions, because NPS and SUS are typically correlated [16]. ### 4.2 Qualitative Results

The thematic analysis on the semi-structured interview answers reinforced the quantitative ﬁnding that participants overwhelmingly liked ASL input. Some participants framed using ASL with an IPA as an issue of equity; for example “my partner is hearing, and so she can speak and get information and I can’t speak, so I have to use methods like touch and I can see that she’ll speak and I have to rely on touch. I feel like I can’t and there is no equity there” (P33). Also, most participants were positive about the LLM-assisted touch interface, but expressed concerns about the latency induced by the time it took to fetch options from ChatGPT. Participants were very negative about head-pointing and felt it did not function well for them; for example “I had to move my face, my head, my neck, my eyes” (P36). But they could see how it may be useful for those who are DeafDisabled where interaction options are even more limited.

Many participants recognized the importance of having hands-free options, but zeroed on ASL as the preferred option. “Yeah. I think it’s important to have a hands-free option. I use my hands for communication, so ASL capturing is okay for short communication, things like turning on the lights” (P36). Another participant suggested a spatial interface: “Maybe like c ontrolling the mouse remotely in a way. Sort of where you are touching the air in front of you, but it’s moving a mouse on the actual screen of the device” (P44).

Most participants were positive about the LLM-assisted touch interface. “It was easy. It was eﬀective. It was fast, it was good. Very simple. No impact on my eyes. It was good. ## 5 Discussion and Conclusion

Addressing RQ1, our ﬁndings indicate that the usability of LLM-assisted touch is close to that of hypothetical ASL input. This mirrors the ﬁndings in related work on LLM-assisted touch vs speech options [5]. However, there was unambiguous enthusiasm for IPAs with sign language recognition, as reﬂected in the NPS scores. This ﬁnding mirrors the higher enthusiasm for speech as a natural language option in the same prior work, as well as higher enthusiasm for ASL in other past work [6].

The enthusiasm is further reﬂected in the post-experiment questionnaires, where ASL was every participant’s favorite input method. This ﬁnding diﬀers from the one that compared speech to LLM-assisted touch; in that work, nearly half of the users indicated a preference for touch [5]. It is possible that this diﬀerence arises from the unique role that ASL plays as the natural language of the US DHH community. The semi-structured interviews underscored this perspective further: providing ASL is not just what DHH people want, but also a matter of equity as per our participant responses. In addition, just like i n related work, LLM latencies have been highlighted as a major usability problem; however, this problem could be solved through smart implementation strategies, such as prefetching responses [5].

Addressing RQ2, head-pointing was frustrating for most participants, suggesting a need for major improvements in usability. However, headpointing also was perceived as an important accessibility option for DeafDisabled people. It is notable that participants volunteered this consideration without being prompted, displaying heightened community awareness and a need for DHHcentric research to include intersectional disabilities and identities. There further is a need for investigating alternative hands-free options. As reported in the results, one participant suggested a mouse-alike interface in 3D space driven by gestures, which may be a promising avenue for future work and more immediately achievable than robust sign language recognition. Eye gaze also deserves another look, based on past work [15].

Overall, with respect to both RQ1 and RQ2, our ﬁndings as of now, reinforce that there is no substitute for oﬀering natural language-based options across the board, no matter whether ASL or ASR on deaf-accented speech, for hands-free IPA interaction. However, for as long as ASL input to IPAs remains out of reach for commercial systems, it still is necessary to continue to explore hands-free alternatives, and LLM-assisted options remain a promising basis for augmenting potential spatial or eye gaze-based interfaces.
